rows.12:1498:
Heh heh... So you like sci-fi and horror?
You have rather bad taste, don't you?{p}
rows.12:14f4:
I don't much care for that type of film myself.
Above all, they have no class.
The story is just tacked on as an afterthought, and far too many of them rely on nothing but visual shocks and special effects.
...But movies are frightening, aren't they?
No, I don't mean horror movies.
I mean film itself.
Don't you think so?
People have long said that photographs steal a person's soul, haven't they?
Nowadays we laugh that off as superstition, but back then people seriously believed it.
That every photo taken of you shortened your life, or that when three people are photographed together, the one in the middle dies young.
Back then, I suppose photography must have seemed utterly uncanny.
Your own image, sealed inside a single sheet of paper.
It truly was magic.
And so everyone feared it.
It's the same with movies.
When movies were first born, they caused quite a stir.
For example, a character in a film fires a gun right at the screen, you see?
They say the audience watching it fainted, thinking they'd been shot dead.
People even believed that other people lived beyond that silver screen, and that they were watching the world those people lived in.
Nowadays no one believes that, of course.
...But is it really a lie?
Was what people believed back then truly just their imagination?
I can't quite bring myself to think so.
Sometimes film captures things that should never be filmed, or strange things that don't exist in reality...
I can't shake the feeling that film has that kind of uncanny power.
What I'm about to tell you is the story of one such movie.{p}
rows.12:24fc:
And so filming began on the society's memorable first production.
I think it was right around this time last year.
...You said you like horror and sci-fi movies, didn't you?
As it happens, so did he.
The movie he set out to make was a horror film titled 'The Mummy Man and the Beauty.'
Now, don't laugh at the title.
What he wanted to make wasn't one of today's SFX films loaded with special effects; if anything, he wanted to make an old-fashioned monster movie from the golden age.
Not that he could have pulled off flashy special effects even if he'd tried.
So instead of fussing over that sort of thing, he poured himself into dark direction and atmosphere, so that even a cheap monster in a simple costume and makeup would look real.{p}
rows.12:3398:
Of course, the detective was played by one of the film society members.
The death scene they had actually shot was a simple one.
The detective, attacked by the mummy, runs away.
The mummy's hands reach for the detective's neck, and the screen goes black.
Then comes the detective's scream.{p}
rows.12:4290:
...I'm sure you've guessed by now.
The girl who played the heroine was found brutally murdered.
They say her body was in pieces.
Of course, I never heard the details, but Tokita knew.
What state the body was in, and how she was killed.
And that the proof was all recorded on that reel.
It was after school that very day, as I recall.
Tokita came up to me and told me how realistic and amazing this movie was.{p}
rows.12:48f4:
The clapperboard filled the screen, and the acting began.
One blown take followed another, the same scene repeating again and again.
It's fascinating, you know.
"...Ah!"{p}
rows.12:4ca8:
"It's going to kill me!
If I don't stop it fast, the mummy's going to kill me!
Everyone dies.
Everyone who gets attacked in this film really dies!"
Tokita screamed in a trembling voice.
Honestly, I didn't understand.
And then, at that very moment,
he told me the secret of this film.
If someone told you something like that, could you believe it?
I'm sorry, but I couldn't.
People dying exactly the way it happened in a film? Surely not.
On the screen, Tokita was quaking with terror.
Just like the real one standing right in front of me...
"Eeeeek!"{p}
rows.12:5b5c:
After that, I started watching the film at regular intervals.
As if I were observing it.
As the months went by, Tokita turned completely into a skeleton.
And before I knew it, there was no one on the screen anymore.
The bones were cleanly gone too, whether they'd crumbled away or someone had cleared them up.
Not a single bone was left.
Just the empty audiovisual room, shown flatly, on and on.
But when I looked closely, it wasn't so.
I was wrong to think no one was there.
Right beside the spot where Tokita's body had been, someone was standing blankly.{p}
rows.12:64ec:
...You dislike them?
I see. That's a shame.
French films do choose their audience, after all.
Whenever I ask people if they like French films, they all tell me the images are beautiful.
But most of them say they can't understand what the film is about, or what's so interesting about it...
Sadly...
By the way, {a}, could it be that you dislike movies in general?{p}
rows.12:751c:
"The Mummy Man... So this was a film after all?"
By now, he was in the mood for watching a film.
He was watching the cruel scenes unfolding on the video with an appreciative eye.
He had already broken free of the delusion that it was real footage of today.
Then the video ended.{p}
rows.12:762c:
For a while, Tokita just sat there in a daze.
Because amid the clumsy direction, there had been scenes with a force unlike anything he had ever seen.
The Mummy Man had chased a high school girl and mercilessly torn her apart until she died.
"It must be an indie film.
If the school is the setting, someone connected with the school must have made it."
Once he thought that, he couldn't rest until he had found the tape's owner.
He wanted to see what came next... no, he wanted to see the finished film. With that thought, he went to bed.
And it was already starting to get light by the time he finally drifted off to sleep.{p}
rows.12:7978:
There on the ground, off in a corner, lay a scrap of bandage.
At that moment, Tokita understood.
The footage on that video had really happened.
And from then on, he couldn't get the scenes from that video out of his head.
Apparently the police investigated the murder as the work of a deranged person.
But Tokita alone was certain the truth of the case lay elsewhere.{p}
